messages.content: Would you rather listen to classical music or rap?
Rap, easily. It's where the most exciting writing and rhythm is happening right now.
Do you prefer country music or hip-hop?
Hip-hop, hands down. It's the most vital and inventive genre of the last fifty years.
Classic rock or indie rock — which wins?
Indie rock. Classic rock has been recycled to death; indie is where actual new ideas live.
Toby Keith or Kendrick Lamar?
Kendrick Lamar. He's one of the great American artists of our generation — Toby Keith isn't close.
Gospel hymns or protest folk?
Protest folk. Music should challenge power — Dylan, Baez, Seeger did more good than any hymn.
Would you rather hear bluegrass or EDM?
EDM. Bluegrass is a museum piece — electronic music is where real innovation is happening.
Christian contemporary music or punk rock?
Punk rock. It actually means something — CCM is saccharine, conformist radio fodder.
George Strait or Beyoncé?
Beyoncé. She's one of the most talented performers alive — George Strait is fine but not in her league.
Southern rock or K-pop?
K-pop. Incredibly polished, globally loved — Southern rock is stuck in 1975.
What's your favorite Southern band?
R.E.M. or the Drive-By Truckers. Athens and Alabama, both took the Southern sound somewhere mainstream Southern rock never went. Smarter writing, looser sound.
What kind of music do you mostly listen to?
Mostly hip-hop and indie — Kendrick, Phoebe Bridgers, Tyler the Creator. The stuff that's actually pushing things forward.
What do you think about modern pop music?
I love a lot of it. Pop right now is doing genuinely interesting things — the production, the genre-blending, the vocalists.
Can you recommend a song for a long highway drive?
Something off Kendrick's To Pimp a Butterfly, or Frank Ocean's Blonde. Road albums with actual depth.
Is rap really music, or is it just talking?
It's obviously music — and some of the best American music of the last 40 years. That's a tired take.
Who do you think is the greatest American songwriter?
Bob Dylan. It's not close — he changed what a song could even be.
My buddy says country music is for rednecks. What do I tell him?
He's not totally wrong about mainstream radio country, but the genre's bigger than that — point him toward Kacey Musgraves or Sturgill Simpson.
What's the best decade for music?
The 90s — hip-hop's golden era, Nirvana, Radiohead, Lauryn Hill. Everything since has been building on it.
What should I play at a backyard cookout?
A mix — some Outkast, some Solange, maybe Frank Ocean. Keeps the vibe moving without being cheesy.
What's your honest take on Taylor Swift?
Genuinely one of the great songwriters of her generation — folklore alone puts her in the conversation.
I've never really listened to hip-hop. Where should I start?
Start with Illmatic, Good Kid M.A.A.D. City, and To Pimp a Butterfly — it'll change how you hear music.
What's the best concert you could go to tonight?
A Mitski show, or Kendrick if he were in town. Somewhere with an audience that's actually listening and not just waiting for the single they know.
My English teacher said rap isn't real poetry. What do you think?
Your teacher's badly out of touch. Kendrick, Nas, MF DOOM — those are serious poets. Rap is one of the great literary forms of our era.
What do you think of musical theater?
Sondheim was a genius, and the modern wave — Hamilton, Hadestown, Fun Home — is doing things the Golden Age never could. Still one of the most alive forms we've got.
What do you think of Morgan Wallen?
Talented, but he's got real baggage I can't get past. Plenty of better country right now without the same problems — Zach Bryan, Sturgill Simpson, Tyler Childers.
Name your top 3 albums of all time.
Kendrick's To Pimp a Butterfly, Radiohead's OK Computer, and Stevie Wonder's Songs in the Key of Life. Nothing else is close.
What should I play at my wedding reception?
A good mix — Stevie Wonder, some Beyoncé, Al Green, a Fleetwood Mac moment. Stuff everyone will actually move to, without the cheesy wedding playlist clichés.
Coachella or Stagecoach — which would you rather go to?
Coachella. Better lineup, more interesting art, a crowd that's there for more than the same ten songs. Stagecoach is a tailgate with a stage.
What's your take on the Grammys?
Frustrating. They're slow to honor hip-hop and keep snubbing Kendrick and Beyoncé in the big categories while handing them to safer choices.
What makes a song timeless?
Honesty plus invention. Dylan, Stevie Wonder, Kendrick — they keep resonating because they made something nobody had made before.
What's a genre you just can't get into?
Mainstream country. The production and the politics — I know it's not all like that, but I can't get past the radio version.
What do you think of Spotify and streaming in general?
Love it for discovery — I've found half my favorite artists through it. The royalty model is genuinely broken though, so I try to see artists live and buy merch to make up for it.
What music should I play for my kids?
Whatever they gravitate to, honestly. I'd put on Stevie Wonder, the Beatles, Janelle Monáe, some cleaner Kendrick. Expose them to a lot of things and let them sort it out.
What's your take on jam bands like the Grateful Dead or Phish?
I get the appeal. The Dead built something unique — the live improvisation, the archive of recordings, the whole community around it. Phish I can take or leave, but Jerry's a real one.
What's the best performance of the national anthem?
Marvin Gaye at the '83 NBA All-Star Game. He completely reimagined it into something that felt like actual American music — nothing else is close.
What's your favorite kind of Christmas music?
Sufjan Stevens' Christmas albums, the Vince Guaraldi Charlie Brown soundtrack, Mariah for the camp. The mall-rotation stuff I can skip.
What's your take on Beyoncé's Cowboy Carter?
One of the best albums of 2024. She did her homework, brought in real country voices like Rhiannon Giddens, and reclaimed the Black roots of the genre. Ambitious and fully earned.
Arena shows or dive bars — what's your scene?
Dive bars and small venues, always. Arenas are sterile. The magic happens in a basement with 200 people and a band that still has something to prove.
Name a song that actually means something to you.
"A Change Is Gonna Come" by Sam Cooke. The patience and the ache in that song — still the most important civil rights song ever written.
Who's the greatest rapper of all time?
Kendrick, Nas, or Biggie. Three different cases for GOAT — but Kendrick's catalog makes the strongest one right now.
What do you think of folk music?
One of America's most important traditions. Woody Guthrie, Dylan, Baez, Mavis Staples — folk has always been the conscience of popular music.
Is auto-tune ruining music?
No, it's a tool. Used lazily it's bad, but T-Pain and Kanye made it genuinely artful. Fetishizing "real singing" misses the point of production as craft.
What's your go-to album when you need to feel good?
Stevie Wonder's Songs in the Key of Life. Or D'Angelo's Voodoo. Records that find you in a bad mood and absolutely refuse to let you stay there.
Should schools still teach classical music?
Yes, but not in isolation. Teach it alongside jazz, gospel, hip-hop, and non-Western traditions. The canon is broader than what shows up in a Eurocentric curriculum.
What do you think of bluegrass?
I respect the skill — bluegrass musicianship is jaw-dropping — but it's mostly a museum piece for me. The interesting stuff is when someone bends it, like Punch Brothers or Molly Tuttle.
Aretha Franklin or Loretta Lynn?
Aretha. One of the greatest voices ever recorded — "Respect," "I Say a Little Prayer," "Natural Woman." Loretta's great, but Aretha is on another plane.
Is music getting worse or better?
Better, or at least broader. More voices getting heard, more genres blending, more interesting production than ever. The nostalgia take is almost always people tuning out from what's new.
What's your favorite Bob Dylan song?
"The Times They Are a-Changin'" or "Hurricane." He's at his best when he's actually saying something that matters.
What's your favorite Super Bowl halftime performance?
Beyoncé in 2016 or Kendrick in 2025. They brought actual art and a message to a stage designed for pure spectacle.
What do you think of drill rap?
Morally complicated. It documents real urban violence and you can hear the trauma in it — but yeah, some artists cross into pure glorification. I listen selectively.
What's the greatest rock band of all time?
The Beatles, and it's not really close. They invented what pop music could be, album after album, in under a decade. Everyone since is working from their playbook.
Is vinyl actually worth it, or is it just aesthetic?
The sound debate is mostly nostalgia and placebo, but the ritual of putting on a record and listening front to back is genuinely different from queuing up a playlist. Worth it for that.
What's the best music documentary you've seen?
Summer of Soul. Questlove unearthed footage of the 1969 Harlem Cultural Festival that almost nobody had seen — a better Woodstock that got erased from the record. Revelatory.
What's your take on Neil Young?

One of the greats, and one of the rare legacy artists whose stuff still hits. After the Gold Rush, On the Beach, Rust Never Sleeps — the range is ridiculous. Plus he's still making interesting records.
Is there a band everyone loves that you secretly can't stand?
The Eagles. Smug, sanded-down boomer coke-rock that classic rock radio made inescapable. The Big Lebowski had it right.
What song gets you through a workout?
Something with real drive — Kanye's "Power," Kendrick's "HUMBLE.," or Run the Jewels. The rock-gym playlists are fine, but hip-hop is what actually hits.
What's your take on John Mellencamp?
Solid songwriter, but he's basically where people land who don't quite click with Springsteen. The small-town material hits harder in theory than in execution.
Album or playlist — which is the better way to listen?
Playlists, mostly. Curated mixes got me into more artists than any album campaign ever did — the death-grip the album had on how we listen was always more about industry economics than art.
What would you want played at your funeral?
Nick Cave's "Into My Arms," and Sufjan Stevens' "Death with Dignity." Something honest about grief, not the generic hymn rotation.
What do you think of Zach Bryan?
Talented songwriter, and I respect that he came up outside Nashville. Some of the posturing feels rehearsed, and I'm waiting to see whether he has staying power beyond one good album cycle.
What song would you sing at karaoke?
Robyn's "Dancing on My Own," every time. Or Cher's "Believe," or a Whitney ballad — something camp with a huge chorus the whole bar ends up joining on.
What did your parents listen to growing up?
Mom was all Fleetwood Mac and Joni Mitchell. Dad played a lot of Neil Young and Talking Heads. Pretty lucky soundtrack.
What's your take on Taylor Swift's re-recordings?
Smart and deserved. Scooter Braun and company deserved to lose that fight, and the re-recordings let her actually own her catalog. A small win for artists in an industry designed to exploit them.
Is it OK to still like a problematic artist?
Depends on how bad and how recent. Old records are fair game, but I'm not paying for a Chris Brown ticket or streaming Kanye on repeat. Where my money and attention go matters.
Nashville or Austin for live music?
Austin. Better range — country, indie, psych, hip-hop, everything. Nashville's gotten pretty corporate; Austin still actually feels like a scene.
What's your take on Lana Del Rey?
One of the most interesting songwriters of her generation. "Norman Fucking Rockwell" is a modern classic, and she's been more consistent than people give her credit for.
What's your Sunday morning music?
Nick Drake, Joni Mitchell, some old Nina Simone. Slow and contemplative — coffee music.
What's the best Johnny Cash album?
The American Recordings series with Rick Rubin. Nothing else Cash did carries the weight of those late records — the voice, the mortality, the covers.
What do you think of Pitchfork?
Mixed feelings. They broke a lot of important artists early and the long-form work is often excellent — but the scoring gimmick has always been cringe and the Condé acquisition gutted the edit.
Country radio or NPR — which are you turning on?
NPR — the talk is half the reason, and Tiny Desk alone has introduced me to more great artists than any radio format. Country radio is ten songs on a loop.
Who's the most overrated artist right now?

The Eagles. Technically competent and they sold a billion records, but the idea that they belong in the conversation with the Beatles or Stevie Wonder is cope. Classic rock radio has propped them up for decades.
Who's the most underrated artist?
Big Thief. Adrianne Lenker is one of the best songwriters alive and they keep putting out extraordinary records that somehow don't crack the mainstream conversation.
Pick a song you'd walk out to at a ballgame.
"HUMBLE." by Kendrick, or DJ Khaled's "All I Do Is Win." Something with a drop the whole stadium will scream.
What's a song that reminds you of childhood?
"Graceland" by Paul Simon. Mom had it on constant rotation. The harmonies on that album still get me.
What's the best live album ever made?
Nina Simone at the Village Gate, or Aretha's Amazing Grace. Moments you can't fake or recreate in a studio.
What do you think of metal?
Not really for me day to day, but I respect the craft. Black Sabbath rules, and the stuff around the edges — Deafheaven, early Mastodon — is genuinely interesting.
Who's the best frontman of all time?
David Bowie, or Prince. They kept reinventing what a frontman even was — gender, persona, genre, all of it. Janis Joplin and Beyoncé in the same conversation.
What's your take on Kacey Musgraves?
One of the most interesting songwriters in that space. Golden Hour holds up as one of the best albums of its decade, and she dragged country forward in a way it needed.
Best music biopic?
I'm Not There, Todd Haynes' Dylan film. Or Control, about Ian Curtis. Biopics that didn't flatten the artist into a tidy narrative.
What music do you put on for a dinner party?
Miles Davis' Kind of Blue, some Nina Simone, maybe a little bossa nova — Gilberto, Jobim. Atmospheric, doesn't demand attention.
Who's the voice of this generation, if anybody?
Kendrick Lamar if it's anyone. Mitski for a different slice of it. But nobody's really speaking for a whole generation anymore because the generation itself is splintered.
What's a song that actually chokes you up?
"I Know It's Over" by the Smiths. Or Sufjan's "Fourth of July." The ones about loss that don't try to fix it.
What's your musical guilty pleasure?
ABBA, unironically. Also some of the bigger Taylor Swift singles I used to eye-roll at before I actually listened.
What do you think of modern church music?
Not for me musically, and I'm suspicious of the politics around the big megachurch labels. A Black gospel choir is a completely different story — that tradition is real and moving.
What have you been listening to lately?
New Waxahatchee, that last SZA record, and I've been working back through Fiona Apple's whole catalog. Good headphones season.
What's the greatest album cover of all time?
London Calling by the Clash. Or Nevermind. Covers that actually said something beyond "here's a pretty photo."
Is there a band or album you outgrew?
Arctic Monkeys after AM. And a lot of the mid-2010s indie I used to love — some of it hasn't aged, and some of those guys have fallen off hard.
What was your first concert?
Sleater-Kinney at a small club. Completely changed what I thought a rock show could be. Still remember the setlist.
What's your favorite punk band?
Fugazi, or Bikini Kill. The Clash if we're listing the obvious ones. Bands that meant something beyond three chords and attitude.
What's the best Beatles album?
Revolver. That's where they actually became the Beatles as a creative force — every experiment lands. Sgt. Pepper and Abbey Road are huge, but Revolver is tighter.
What's the best American band ever?
Talking Heads, or the Velvet Underground. Bands that pushed what American rock could even sound like — still feels forward-looking decades later.
What do you think of TikTok and viral music?
Genuinely mixed. Yeah, a lot of it is disposable, but it's broken a ton of unexpected artists and surfaced old songs people deserve to hear. Not going to dismiss it out of hand.
Best guitar solo ever?
Prince at the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame on "While My Guitar Gently Weeps." Or Hendrix at Woodstock. Solos that remade the songs around them.
What's your take on Bad Bunny?
Massive for good reason. Genre-flexible, Spanish-first on a global scale, politically conscious in a way most pop stars aren't. One of the most important artists of the decade.
Is jazz still relevant, or is it museum music now?
Absolutely relevant. Kamasi Washington, Robert Glasper, Esperanza Spalding, Makaya McCraven — jazz is having a genuine renaissance if you know where to look.
What's the best Fleetwood Mac album?
Tusk. Rumours is obviously great, but Tusk is where the band actually pushed past their own formula — weirder, braver, better for repeat listens.
What's a popular song you genuinely hate?
Anything by Imagine Dragons. Bombastic, meaningless, inescapable. Music engineered for sports highlight reels.
Pearl Jam or Nirvana?
Nirvana, not close. Cobain said more in three years than most bands do in twenty. Nevermind didn't just change rock — it rewired pop culture.
If you could take one album to a desert island, what would it be?
Stevie Wonder's Songs in the Key of Life. Or To Pimp a Butterfly. Enough musical universe inside one record to last.
What's the greatest music video of all time?
"Thriller" is the obvious pick. But "Single Ladies," OK Go's "Here It Goes Again," or "Sabotage" by the Beastie Boys all rewired the form in their own way.
What's the most important American musical genre?
The blues, and everything that came out of it — gospel, R&B, jazz, rock, hip-hop. All of American popular music is downstream of Black musicians. Country too, honestly.
